citation.title: On being sane in insane places.

identity.note: Zotero parent TSN2F24F matched the primary article and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 1 curriculum names Rosenhan 1973.

appraisal.studyDesign: Two-part covert field experiment and institutional observation across psychiatric hospitals.
appraisal.population: Eight known-sane pseudopatients sought admission to 12 hospitals; a later expectancy phase involved staff judgments on 193 genuine admissions when no pseudopatients were sent.
appraisal.comparator: Known-sane status and normal post-admission behavior versus hospital diagnostic judgments; later staff suspicions were compared with the fact that no pseudopatients were presented.
appraisal.outcomes: Pseudopatients were not detected as sane, all except one were admitted with schizophrenia, and stays lasted 7-52 days; in the expectancy phase, staff flagged genuine patients despite zero pseudopatients.
appraisal.limitations: Small purposive and deceptive sample; the article cautions that pseudopatients cannot represent true patients' subjective experiences, and the second phase could not determine the true status of suspected patients.

citation.title: Effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs in patients with chronic schizophrenia.
citation.organization: Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness (CATIE) Investigators
citation.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

identity.note: Zotero parent 2TPA9P9D matched the PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 2 curriculum names CATIE.

appraisal.studyDesign: Multisite, double-blind randomized comparative-effectiveness trial lasting up to 18 months.
appraisal.population: 1,493 patients with schizophrenia recruited at 57 U.S. sites; 1,432 received at least one dose.
appraisal.comparator: Olanzapine, perphenazine, quetiapine, risperidone, and, after FDA approval, ziprasidone.
appraisal.outcomes: Seventy-four percent discontinued assigned treatment before 18 months; olanzapine had longer persistence than some agents but greater weight and metabolic effects, while perphenazine had similar effectiveness to several newer agents and more extrapyramidal effects.
appraisal.limitations: Very high discontinuation limits long-term outcome ascertainment; time to discontinuation combines efficacy, tolerability, and other reasons rather than isolating symptom efficacy.

citation.title: Acute and longer-term outcomes in depressed outpatients requiring one or several treatment steps: a STAR*D report.

identity.note: Zotero parent LGJ9CSR3 matched the PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 2 curriculum names STAR*D.

appraisal.studyDesign: Multicenter sequenced effectiveness-trial report covering one to four acute treatment steps and a 12-month naturalistic follow-up.
appraisal.population: Broadly representative adults with nonpsychotic major depressive disorder treated as outpatients; N=3,671 at step 1 and N=123 at step 4.
appraisal.comparator: Outcomes across successive treatment steps among patients who failed to remit or could not tolerate a preceding step; no single fixed parallel comparator spans all four steps.
appraisal.outcomes: QIDS-SR remission rates were 36.8%, 30.6%, 13.7%, and 13.0% across steps 1-4, with reported cumulative remission of 67%; needing more steps was associated with higher relapse during follow-up.
appraisal.limitations: Later-step estimates come from progressively smaller, selected subsets, and the follow-up phase was naturalistic.

citation.title: Influence of family life on the course of schizophrenic disorders: a replication.

identity.note: Zotero parent E8BCCFSN matched the primary article and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal; the publisher supplies Birley's middle initial T.

curriculum.mappingNote: Tier 1 and Zotero identify Brown, Birley, and Wing 1972; the tracked Week 4 page names Brown 1962. Faculty decision required; neither source was rewritten.

appraisal.studyDesign: Prospective, nonrandomized nine-month follow-up study in which family emotional measures, prior patient behavior, and later relapse were assessed independently.
appraisal.population: 101 patients aged 18-64 with possible or probable schizophrenia, selected from people living with relatives in the Camberwell catchment plus a recent-illness Bexley group.
appraisal.comparator: High versus low relative expressed emotion, with analyses also considering face-to-face contact, medication, prior disturbance, and other clinical and social factors.
appraisal.outcomes: Thirty-five patients relapsed; high relative expressed emotion was associated with relapse during the nine months after discharge, and the association persisted after adjustment for measured background factors.
appraisal.limitations: The exposure could not be randomized; the authors could not determine whether relative expressed emotion caused later behavior, reflected earlier patient behavior, or was reciprocal, and the restricted cohort limits generalizability.

appraisal.studyDesign: Rating-scale and screening-instrument development with interrater reliability and diagnostic-agreement testing, plus a consecutive-admission prevalence assessment.
appraisal.population: Forty-four simultaneous ratings of 28 cases meeting the 14-item screen threshold; separately, 215 consecutive admissions to one academic psychiatric inpatient facility.
appraisal.comparator: Agreement between raters and diagnostic agreement with catatonia criteria proposed by other authors; no treatment comparator.
appraisal.outcomes: A 23-item scale and 14-item screen had total-score interrater reliabilities of 0.93 and 0.95, respectively; 15 of 215 consecutive admissions met catatonia criteria.
appraisal.limitations: Reliability testing involved only 28 cases and prevalence came from one academic inpatient site; diagnostic agreement used existing criteria rather than an independent gold standard or prospective outcomes.

citation.title: A meta-analysis of outcome studies comparing bona fide psychotherapies: Empirically, "all must have prizes."

identity.note: Zotero parent PDWXBEMZ matched the primary article title, first author, year, DOI, and journal; no PMID is assigned.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 3 curriculum names Wampold 1997.

appraisal.studyDesign: Meta-analysis of direct outcome-study comparisons between bona fide psychotherapies drawn from six journals.
appraisal.population: Participants represented in included comparative psychotherapy outcome studies; the abstract does not report a pooled sample size or diagnostic composition.
appraisal.comparator: Bona fide psychotherapies directly compared with other bona fide psychotherapies.
appraisal.outcomes: Between-treatment effect sizes were homogeneous around zero; even under liberal assumptions the upper bound of the true difference was about 0.20, supporting roughly equivalent efficacy across included comparisons.
appraisal.limitations: The evidence base was limited to direct comparisons found in six journals; pooled participant and diagnostic details were not reported in the abstract, so the result should not be generalized to every therapy-problem pairing.

citation.title: Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Chronically Parasuicidal Borderline Patients

identity.note: Zotero parent SHMA7MDE matched the publisher and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 3 curriculum names Linehan 1991.

appraisal.studyDesign: One-year randomized clinical trial with assessments every four months.
appraisal.population: Chronically parasuicidal women meeting criteria for borderline personality disorder.
appraisal.comparator: Dialectical behavior therapy versus community treatment as usual.
appraisal.outcomes: DBT produced fewer and less medically severe parasuicide events, better retention in individual therapy, and fewer inpatient psychiatric days; groups did not differ on depression, hopelessness, suicidal ideation, or reasons for living.
appraisal.limitations: The narrowly selected all-women, chronically parasuicidal borderline-personality sample and one-year horizon limit generalizability; several symptom measures showed no between-group difference.

citation.title: Family intervention for schizophrenia

identity.note: Zotero parent P4M5H9VM and PubMed PMID 21154340 agree on the 2010 update identity and .pub2 DOI; current Cochrane publisher metadata disagrees. Publisher reconciliation remains reserved for controller and faculty resolution.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 4 curriculum names Pharoah 2010.

appraisal.studyDesign: Cochrane systematic review and fixed-effect meta-analysis of 53 randomized or quasi-randomized trials, with searching updated through September 2008.
appraisal.population: People with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or schizophrenia-like conditions and their families in community settings.
appraisal.comparator: Community-oriented family psychosocial intervention versus standard care.
appraisal.outcomes: Family intervention may reduce relapse in 32 RCTs with 2,981 participants (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.50-0.60; NNT 7), may reduce admission and improve medication adherence, and showed no evidence for a suicide effect.
appraisal.limitations: Poor trial methods may overestimate effects; randomization and evaluator blinding were often inadequately described, and small negative studies may have been missed.

citation.title: Fluoxetine, Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, and Their Combination for Adolescents With Depression: Treatment for Adolescents With Depression Study (TADS) Randomized Controlled Trial
citation.organization: Treatment for Adolescents With Depression Study (TADS) Team

identity.note: Zotero parent 6DTR4GC8 matched the publisher and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: Tracked curriculum files do not assign TADS to a week. Zotero suggests Week 2, but that tag is advisory pending faculty confirmation.

appraisal.studyDesign: Twelve-week, four-arm randomized controlled trial at 13 U.S. academic and community clinics; medication and placebo arms were double-blind and CBT-containing arms were unblinded.
appraisal.population: Volunteer sample of 439 adolescents aged 12-17 years with primary DSM-IV major depressive disorder; adolescents at high suicide risk and those with primary substance-use disorders were excluded.
appraisal.comparator: Fluoxetine plus CBT versus fluoxetine alone, CBT alone, and placebo.
appraisal.outcomes: Response was 71.0%, 60.6%, 43.2%, and 34.8%, respectively; combined treatment had the best benefit-risk tradeoff. Suicidal thinking improved in all groups; seven participants attempted suicide and none died by suicide.
appraisal.limitations: Excluding adolescents at high suicide risk and primary substance-use cases limits safety and generalizability; seven suicide attempts were too few, leaving the trial inadequately powered for statistical safety comparison. The 12-week horizon, unblinded CBT conditions, and lack of a CBT-plus-placebo arm also limit inference.

citation.title: Relationship of Childhood Abuse and Household Dysfunction to Many of the Leading Causes of Death in Adults: The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study

identity.note: Zotero parent ZT9DMH79 matched the publisher and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked Week 6 curriculum names Felitti 1998.

appraisal.studyDesign: Questionnaire-based observational analysis using logistic regression to relate retrospectively reported childhood exposures to adult health risks and disease.
appraisal.population: 9,508 respondents (70.5% of 13,494 adult HMO members who had completed a standardized medical evaluation), with 8,056 complete cases analyzed.
appraisal.comparator: Cumulative adverse-childhood-experience categories from 0-7, including comparison of four or more categories with none.
appraisal.outcomes: ACE count showed graded associations with adult health risks and disease; four or more versus no categories was associated with 4- to 12-fold higher risks for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempt.
appraisal.limitations: Retrospective self-report, nonresponse, and an observational baseline analysis permit association rather than causal inference and may limit generalizability beyond this HMO sample.

citation.title: Influence of Life Stress on Depression: Moderation by a Polymorphism in the 5-HTT Gene

curriculum.mappingNote: Tracked curriculum files do not assign Caspi 2003 to a week. Zotero suggests Week 6, but that tag is advisory pending faculty confirmation.

appraisal.studyDesign: Prospective-longitudinal observational study of a representative birth cohort.
appraisal.population: Members of a representative birth cohort assessed for stressful life events, 5-HTT promoter genotype, and depression-related outcomes.
appraisal.comparator: Short-allele carriers with one or two copies versus long-allele homozygotes across levels of stressful life events.
appraisal.outcomes: Short-allele carriers showed more depressive symptoms, diagnosable depression, and suicidality in relation to stressful life events, consistent with a reported gene-by-environment interaction.
appraisal.limitations: This was an observational finding in one cohort; it does not by itself establish causality or independent replication and generalizability.

appraisal.studyDesign: Preregistered association analyses across large population-based and case-control samples.
appraisal.population: Multiple samples ranging from 62,138 to 443,264 participants across subsamples, using several depression phenotypes and environmental moderators.
appraisal.comparator: Main effects and gene-by-environment effects for 18 historical depression candidate genes, with candidate-gene sets also compared with noncandidate genes.
appraisal.outcomes: No clear candidate-polymorphism association or candidate gene-by-environment effect was found; candidate genes as a set were no more associated with depression than noncandidate genes.

citation.title: Risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors: A meta-analysis of 50 years of research.

identity.note: Zotero parent FP88WVWT matched the PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked curriculum maps Franklin 2017 to Week 5.

appraisal.studyDesign: Random-effects meta-analysis of longitudinal predictors of suicidal thoughts and behaviors across 365 studies, 3,428 effect sizes, and 50 years.
appraisal.population: Participants in longitudinal studies predicting later suicidal ideation, attempt, or death; pooled demographic composition was not reported in the abstract.
appraisal.comparator: Risk-factor categories and exposure levels versus later specific suicidal-thought-or-behavior outcomes; no treatment comparator.
appraisal.outcomes: Prediction was only slightly better than chance across odds-ratio, hazard-ratio, and diagnostic-accuracy analyses; no broad category predicted far above chance and accuracy did not improve over 50 years.
appraisal.limitations: The underlying literature used homogeneous risk factors, rarely examined combinations, and had narrow methods. Mean follow-up was nearly 10 years (median 5 years), and fewer than 1% of effects used horizons of one month or less; the meta-analysis may therefore miss short-term dynamic signals and should not be overgeneralized to acute bedside prediction.

citation.title: Neurobiologic Advances from the Brain Disease Model of Addiction

identity.note: Zotero parent 9FCMTHM2 matched the primary article and PubMed title, first author, year, DOI, PMID, and journal.

curriculum.mappingNote: The tracked curriculum maps Volkow 2016 to Week 5.

appraisal.studyDesign: Narrative and conceptual review of neurobiological evidence supporting the brain-disease model of addiction.
appraisal.outcomes: The review synthesizes a three-stage addiction cycle and links it to adaptations in reward, stress, and executive-control circuits that impair behavioral control.
appraisal.limitations: The review has no defined study population, comparator, or pooled clinical-effect estimate; it also notes that the model does not identify an abnormality shared by every person with addiction and does not by itself explain untreated recovery.
